html:
Around 1004 the Byzantine noblewoman Maria Argyropoulina married Giovanni Orseolo, son of the doge of Venice, and she is said to have eaten with a small golden fork. It is often told as the arrival of the table fork in Western Europe.

Maria came from a great family of Constantinople and was a cousin of Basil II. The wedding showed the close ties between Venice and the Byzantine Empire, where small forks for eating were already in use among the rich.

To Venetians such manners seemed shockingly refined. The churchman Peter Damian wrote of a Greek wife of a doge's family who would not touch food with her fingers and had her servants cut it up for her to eat with a golden fork. He presented her early death as God's punishment for luxury. Historians argue whether he meant Maria, who died of plague with her husband and child around 1006, or a later Greek dogaressa.

Forks stayed rare in the West for centuries. They spread in Italy first and became common at tables in northern Europe only in the 17th and 18th centuries.
